title: How to Recharge Your Body’s Antioxidants
description: Every cell in your body carries a rechargeable battery for fighting oxidative stress. It’s called glutathione. Every time it neutralizes a free radical, the glutathione battery drains. And how well your cells recharge it may matter as much as how much of it you have. Now, emerging literature on glutathione shows promise for use cases ranging from reducing wrinkles (yes, mom, don’t worry, I got you) to Parkinson’s disease to liver health. Today, we’ll look at what happens when you top it up from the outside, and at a surprising way to keep the charger running from the inside. What Is Glutathione? Glutathione is a molecule your body naturally produces in virtually every cell. Structurally, it’s made from three amino acids (glutamate, cysteine, and glycine). And functionally, I call it the cell’s “rechargeable battery” for handling oxidative and chemical stress. What do I mean by that? Glutathione can donate electrons to neutralize reactive oxygen species . These are free radicals that can damage proteins, fats, and DNA. I n the process, two glutathione molecules link together to form an oxidized version called GSSG. Then, another enzyme uses energy from a different molecule, NADPH , to convert GSSG back into the active form of glutathione, effectively “recharging” the glutathione battery to be used again. We’ll come back to that recycling system later. I promise. But that’s only one of glutathione’s jobs. Second , glutathione helps recharge other antioxidants, including vitamin C and E. So rather than acting alone, glutathione sits at the hub of an antioxidant network. And third , glutathione plays a central role in detoxification, particularly in the liver.

title: This Brownie Lowered My Blood Sugar (By Accident)
description: I created a brownie that lowered my blood sugar by accident. I say “by accident” because the original purpose of this invention was to do something else: engineer a brownie that would increase my nitric oxide (NO) levels and improve blood flow. And while it appeared successful in that endeavor, I also measured my blood sugar at baseline, 30 minutes, and 60 minutes. It went from 85 → 75 → 73 mg/dL. Then, I tried it again. And my blood sugar dropped from the 80s to the 60s. No spike and drop. Just a clean, smooth decline. After a bit more digging and discovered that one of the ingredients has a double function in the body. It increases levels of a signaling molecule (nitric oxide) that not only supports cardiovascular health, but also improves sugar metabolism and improves insulin sensitivity. So, in this special letter, I’m going to give you not only a biology lesson, but also an epic recipe that will stimulate your neurons and your taste buds. title: What Exercise Really Does to Heart Plaque
description: You can have plaque in your arteries and a healthy heart at the same time. I know that sounds weird, but research suggests that high volumes of exercise can increase coronary artery calcium (CAC), which is hardened plaque in the vessels of your heart. And ordinarily, more calcified plaque and a higher CAC score on cardiac imaging are associated with a greater risk of heart disease . So why would athletes have more calcified plaque? Sounds like a paradox. But it gets weirder! Because even as coronary calcium increases, cardiovascular risk may not… it might even go down. That’s completely the opposite of what we’re taught and seems to defy logic, like a flying hippo. How can more exercise sometimes lead to more plaque in your heart, but not more heart attacks or cardiovascular deaths? Understanding the answer is literally life and death. In fact, it may be the reason I still have a dad. The biology we’re going to discuss may have literally saved his life. I know that sounds like an exaggeration. But it’s not. You’ll see. But let’s get into our first mystery! Paradox #1: When More Exercise Means More Plaque This is one of the most curious paradoxes in exercise physiology. People who perform large volumes of endurance exercise tend to have more CAC than moderately active individuals. To define our terms, when doctors want to know how much plaque is building up in your heart’s arteries, they run a scan that gives you a “coronary artery calcium” score. Think of it like rust in a pipe. More calcium, more buildup. And in the general population, a higher score tracks with a higher risk of heart attacks and death. A CAC of 0, by comparison, is thought of as a warranty against having a heart attack. This has come to be known as the “ Power of Zero.
